item.content:encoded:
The Colorado Rockies are 57–99.
Purple Row After Dark: If the Rockies could steal one player
An absurd rule for absurd times: if the worst team in baseball could steal one player from a playoff club, who should the Rockies take?
One more loss will give them their fourth consecutive 100-loss season, and they are almost certainly going to finish with the worst record in baseball.
These are absurd times for the Rockies, so I have devised an appropriately absurd rule to help them out.
The team with the worst record in baseball gets to steal one player from a playoff team.
There are, naturally, some restrictions. We’re freezing the playoff field as it stood before games on Sunday, September 20. The player has to come from one of those 12 teams, cannot be a pending free agent, and you cannot take the player who leads his team in FanGraphs WAR. The Rockies also inherit the player’s existing contract.
No, one player is not suddenly turning the Rockies into a contender. But could one poached superstar at least keep this thing from becoming five consecutive 100-loss seasons?
Here’s the board:
| Team | Off limits: fWAR leader | Highest available fWAR | Other players worth considering |
| Rays | Junior Caminero (5.2) | Drew Rasmussen (4.7) | Jonathan Aranda (3) |
| Guardians | Parker Messick (4.6) | Steven Kwan (3.4) | Gavin Williams (3.4), Brayan Rocchio (3.3), José Ramírez (2.2) |
| Rangers | Ezequiel Duran (4.6) | Jacob deGrom (4.2) | Josh Jung (2.9), Wyatt Langford (2.8) |
| Yankees | Cam Schlittler (6.1) | Ben Rice (4) | Cody Bellinger (3.9), Aaron Judge (2) |
| Red Sox | Willson Contreras (4.1) | Payton Tolle (4) | Ceddanne Rafaela (3.9), Ranger Suárez (3.7) |
| White Sox | Miguel Vargas (5) | Chase Meidroth (4) | Tristan Peters (3.9), Sean Burke (3.1) |
| Brewers | Jacob Misiorowski (6.3) | Brice Turang (5.4) | Jackson Chourio (4), Jake Bauers (3.6) |
| Dodgers | Shohei Ohtani (6.7) | Yoshinobu Yamamoto (4.7) | Max Muncy (4.3), Andy Pages (3.9) |
| Braves | Chris Sale (5.7) | Michael Harris II (4) | Matt Olson (4), Drake Baldwin (3.1) |
| Cubs | Pete Crow-Armstrong (10.2) | Alex Bregman (5) | Dansby Swanson (3.6) |
| Padres | Fernando Tatis Jr. (5) | Jackson Merrill (4) | Ty France (3.8), Mason Miller (3.7) |
| Phillies | Cristopher Sánchez (5.8) | Jesús Luzardo (5.6) | Zack Wheeler (3.5), Bryce Harper (3.4) |
For me, the choice comes down to Brice Turang, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Aaron Judge.
Turang is probably the sensible choice.
At 5.4 fWAR, he would easily lead the Rockies, giving them a legitimate top-end player while immediately solving second base for the foreseeable future. He’s 26, hitting .266/.367/.441 with an .808 OPS, and brings value on both sides of the ball with elite range, strong baserunning and a 95th-percentile walk rate.
It would be a very easy way to make the roster better.
But the Rockies really need starting pitching.
Enter Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
He’s 14–8 with a 2.51 ERA, 178 strikeouts and a 0.87 WHIP over 179 innings. His Statcast profile is just as impressive: 100th-percentile pitching run value, 99th-percentile fastball run value, 95th-percentile offspeed run value and a 91st-percentile xERA.
Pitchers are risky, and Yamamoto comes with a lot of money attached. But it’s hard to argue with either the profile or the results, and the addition of the Penner family makes absorbing that contract a lot easier to imagine.
Speaking of high-priced items...
Aaron Judge.
Judge being available is basically a loophole created by our own stupid rule. Injuries have limited him to just 285 plate appearances, which is why he sits at only 2 fWAR, but he’s still hitting .241/.360/.511 with 15 home runs.
And the underlying numbers are still very much Judge: a .396 xwOBA, .569 xSLG, 94.0 mph average exit velocity and a 57.5% hard-hit rate.
It is very hard to look at that and say, “No thanks.”
After all, Aaron Judge is the type of hitter that, if he were playing 81 games a year at Coors Field, I might take out a small loan for season tickets.
So who are you stealing?

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK (AP) — Cristopher Sánchez earned his major league-leading 18th win Sunday, leading the Philadelphia Phillies to a 7-2 victory over the New York Mets.
The Phillies (86-70), who salvaged a split of the four-game series, entered Sunday in the third National League wild-card spot, one game behind the Chicago Cubs and San Diego Padres and four games clear of the Arizona Diamondbacks.
Sánchez surrendered six hits — including Bo Bichette’s sixth-inning homer — and struck out six over 6 1/3 innings as he snapped a tie with the Boston Red Sox’s Sonny Gray for the big league lead in wins.

Already have an account? Log in to continue.
Otherwise, follow the link below to join.
| Please log in to continue |
The last Phillies pitcher to lead the majors in wins was Steve Carlton with 23 in 1982.
Justin Crawford had a three-run triple and Luis Arraez finished with two RBIs. Alec Bohm and Trea Turner each had run-scoring hits. Kyle Schwarber tied a career high with four walks.
Rookie Jonah Tong (2-2) gave up four runs and struck out five in 4 2/3 innings for the last-place Mets, who finished 36-45 at home — their worst record at Citi Field since the 2013 team went 33-48.
PIRATES 4, ROYALS 3
PITTSBURGH (AP) — Rafael Flores Jr. hit the go-ahead two-run home run in the eighth inning to help Pittsburgh to a win over Kansas City and complete a series sweep.
After Ryan O’Hearn led off with a single to center, Flores sent a slider from Nate Pearson (2-3) into the left-field bleachers for his 10th homer this season.
Pittsburgh rallied with a two-run homer in the eighth for a second straight day. Brandon Lowe had his 33rd of the season in a 6-5 win Saturday.
Carmen Mlodzinki (8-7) got the win. He allowed two runs and three hits in three innings. The reliever gave up a pinch-hit, two-run home run to Vinnie Pasquantino that gave Kansas City a 3-2 lead with two outs in the seventh.
Mason Montgomery earned his 16th save. He retired the first two batters in the ninth before Luke Maile hit a double and took third on a fielding error by Jake Mangum. Montgomery got Isaac Collins to fly out to right to strand Maile.
The Royals went ahead 1-0 in the first inning with three straight singles off Lake Bachar. Bobby Witt Jr. beat out a groundball to second baseman Lowe. He moved to third on a single to right from Jac Caglianone and scored when Perez shot one through the middle of the infield.
RAYS 5, RED SOX 1
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. (AP) — Griffin Jax tossed five shutout innings and the Tampa Bay crept closer to the AL East title with a victory over Boston.
The Rays will have an opportunity to clinch the franchise’s fifth division title during Tuesday’s doubleheader at the New York Yankees.
Boston would have clinched a playoff spot with a victory. The Red Sox, who were 32-46 and 15 1/2 games back in the AL East on June 24, have since gone 52-25. They could still wrap up a spot Sunday with a Houston loss.
Jax (8-10) allowed three singles and worked out of a bases-loaded jam in the fifth inning by striking out Roman Anthony. Cole Sulser, Brody Hopkins and Steven Matz each pitched an inning of scoreless relief.
Boston’s Trevor Story spoiled the shutout in the ninth with a one-out home run off right-hander Ty Johnson.
The Rays scored four first-inning runs off left-hander Patrick Sandoval (1-7). Jonny DeLuca smashed a two-run, bases-loaded double down the left-field line and Chandler Simpson followed with a two-run single. Sandoval began the inning by walking Yandy Diaz and Ryan Vilade, then surrendering a single to Junior Caminero.
CUBS 9, REDS 1
CINCINNATI (AP) — Pete Crow-Armstrong hit his 45th home run as Chicago moved closer to clinching a postseason berth with a victory over Cincinnati.
Chicago (87-69) reduced its magic number to one and could wrap up a berth if the Diamondbacks lose to the Yankees later Sunday.
The Cubs began the day tied with the Padres and one game ahead of the Phillies for the top NL wild-card spot which would earn them home-field advantage in the wild-card round. The Cubs own the tiebreakers over the Diamondbacks, Padres, and Phillies.
Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman left Sunday’s game in the fourth inning after being struck in the face by a foul ball off the bat of Michael Busch while standing near the on-deck circle.
Cubs left-hander David Peterson (9-8) allowed a run on three hits in seven innings with one walk and seven strikeouts.
The Cubs loaded the bases with one out in the third. Ian Happ singled in a run and Nico Hoerner walked to force in another to extend Chicago’s lead to 3-0. Pedro Ramirez’s two-run single made the score 5-0.
Reds right-hander Rhett Lowder (6-12) allowed five earned runs on six hits with three walks and three strikeouts.
CARDINALS 5, NATIONALS 3
ST. LOUIS (AP) — Iván Herrera hit a pair of home runs, and Leo Bernal also homered as St. Louis scored three runs in the eighth inning to come from behind and beat Washington.
Bernal hit his fifth homer of the season off Yovanny Cruz (0-2) after Erik Tolman walked Jordan Walker with two outs in the eighth inning.
Herrera hit his second homer of the game and 18th of the season to tie the game at 3-all after hitting a solo shot in the first inning.
It was Herrera’s third career multi-homer game and second this season after going deep twice on June 13 at Minnesota.
Luis Gastelum (5-3) pitched a scoreless eighth inning for St. Louis, and Riley O’Brien pitched a perfect ninth to earn his National League-leading 38th save.
Cardinals starter Quinn Mathews allowed three runs on seven hits and two walks in a career-high seven innings.
Jake Irvin allowed two runs on three hits and had eight strikeouts in 5 1/3 innings for the Nationals.

item.content:encoded:
The Yankees’ odds of winning the AL East are down to 2.8 percent per FanGraphs after getting walked off by the Diamondbacks last night. I know mathematically that makes sense, but the chances mentally feel even more extreme. I’ve been having “fun” (or whatever) comping the odds to certain pitchers from history getting a hit. We are the dregs. Remember mid-2000s Mets pitcher Aaron Heilman? I personally remember him most for giving up the homer to Yadier Molina late in Game 7 of the 2006 NLCS, just before Adam Wainwright famously caught Carlos Beltrán looking to win the pennant.
Anyway, Heilman was a horrendous hitter. He singled once in his rookie year, and then never got another hit. He ended his career 1-for-47, so an .021 average. So the Yankees just need magic only a little bit more sufficient than that RBI single by Heilman off Sidney Ponson on August 12, 2003! Hell yeah.
It’s not happening, but we press on because it’s good to check up on what everyone else is doing anyway. Here’s what was going on Saturday.
Tampa Bay Rays (94-60) 2, Boston Red Sox (84-71) 1
The Yankees gained a full game on the Rays on Friday for the first time in over a week, as Boston snapped their six-game winning streak. There was no such fortune to be found yesterday though; Tampa Bay made sure of that well before first pitch in Arizona, and it only got worse from there. By the end of the night, the Rays once again had a five-game lead over the Yanks; Tampa Bay’s magic number (combination of Rays wins or Yankees losses) to clinch the AL East is four.
This one was a pitchers’ duel to the bitter end. Brayan Bello had easily his best outing of a turbulent season (and probably the best of his career), firing eight shutout frames at the Trop and fanning 11 Rays, tying a personal best from July 9, 2024. As he only went 5.1 in that one and faced merely the soon-to-depart-Oakland A’s rather than the division-leading Rays.
The only true blemish on Bello’s record came when Jonathan Aranda cracked an opposite-field homer to make it a 1-1 game in the fourth. Tampa Bay had a chance to make it 2-1 against Bello in the seventh when Liam Hicks and Chandler Simpson led off with singles. Bello then induced a grounder from Victor Mesa Jr. to move up the runners, and then another off the bat of Richie Palacios to Trevor Story, who nailed pinch-runner Jonny DeLuca at home. Palacios swiped second, but Bello fanned Cedric Mullins to end the inning. The Rays went down in order in the eighth to end Bello’s brilliant night.
Unfortunately for Bello, a win wasn’t in the cards because Boston put up next to nothing against Freddy Peralta and the Rays’ pitching staff. Doubles by Caleb Durbin and Roman Anthony gave the Red Sox their one run in the second, but they were stymied from there. They had chances!
- Second inning after Anthony’s two-out double: Mickey Gasper lineout to center
- Fourth inning with runners on first and second, one out: Story strikeout, Durbin popout
- Fifth inning with runner on second, one out: Anthony groundout, Gasper strikeout
- Sixth inning with runners on first and second, two out: Durbin fly out to left
- Eighth inning after Adley Rutschman’s one-out double: Wilyer Abreu strikeout, Nick Sogard lineout
Even against lockdown Rays closer Bryan Baker, Boston had one last shot to take a late lead. After Story grounded out, Durbin lined a double down the left field line to put himself in scoring position for Jarren Duran. Durbin darted from second, however, and got thrown out stealing third. Duran promptly followed with a triple over DeLuca’s head in center. Isiah Kiner-Falefa bounced one to Junior Caminero at third to end the threat.
Granted a chance to walk it off, Tampa Bay didn’t waste it. Rather than blasting a homer to finish the game as he had twice earlier this homestand, Caminero began the ninth against Garrett Whitlock with a single to left. (A catwalk curtailed Durbin’s effort to catch a popup earlier in the AB.) DeLuca popped up, but Chandler Simpson grounded one through the six-hole for another hit. The runners moved up when catcher Connor Wong let a Whitlock sinker up bounce off his glove for a passed ball. Palacios ended the night with flare to center that fell in, securing the win for Tampa Bay. At least the Wild Card Series is also almost certainly going to be at Yankee Stadium now, I suppose.
AL Rock Fight
Cleveland Guardians (80-75) 12, The Athletics (61-94) 6
Two crooked numbers effectively decided Saturday’s affair with the A’s in a hurry. Tanner Bibee kind of stunk and would allow six runs in a dozen hits while failing to make through five, but it hardly mattered. Cleveland erased a 2-0 deficit in the first on a three-run shot from rookie Chase DeLauter and two-run homer by Angel Martinez. The A’s got one back in the third, only to see another five-spot from the Guardians on poor Jacob Lopez as David Fry, Austin Hedges, and Brayan Rocchio all delivered RBI doubles. Martinez later added a homer and an RBI single in a career-best four-hit day.
Chicago White Sox (79-76) 3, Detroit Tigers (73-82) 1
Cleveland’s win meant that Chicago was stuck at a game back in the AL Central in the best-case, but they did at least help push one of their Wild Card foes out of the picture with a win. Honestly, this was probably kind of a dud of a game for anyone who isn’t a White Sox fan, the lone highlights being Sean Burke’s six scoreless frames and Miguel Vargas’ sixth-inning solo shot to make it 3-1, Chicago (the other runs scored on an RBI single by Munetaka Murakami and a fifth-inning sac fly). Spencer Torkelson had a chance to tie the game with a homer following Hao-Yu Lee’s two-out single in the ninth, but he flew out to center to end it.
Milwaukee Brewers (97-58) 1, Baltimore Orioles (75-80) 0
Yeah, it’s time to stick a fork in the O’s. It was all but certain for awhile now, but Chicago’s win combined with Baltimore’s second-straight loss to Milwaukee means that the Orioles are four back with a week to play, plus multiple teams in front of them. Trevor Rogers was the hard-luck loser here while Baltimore got blanked on four hits and Rece Hinds lost a fly ball from Joey Ortiz in the sun, allowing him to triple and score on Gary Sánchez’s RBI grounder. Woof.
Texas Rangers (78-77) 6, Toronto Blue Jays (76-79) 1
The O’s aren’t the only bird that are all but shot down, either. Trade Deadline acquisition José Soriano coughed up an early homer to Josh Jung, beginning a five-inning, six-run outing that pushed Toronto three games out in the Wild Card and the Rangers into a one-game AL West lead over Houston. The only downside for Texas was that second-half surprise Cal Quantrill—who has a 1.75 ERA since re-entering the rotation in late July—left in the second with lat tightness, so old friend Jordan Montgomery picked up the slack in long relief, retiring 11 of the 12 hitters he faced with no hits allowed.
Atlanta Braves (91-64) 6, Houston Astros (77-78) 3
Houston and Texas have been wrestling all week over the prestigious “Who can win this horri-awful division with a .500-ish record” crown. Sunday it went to Texas with the Astros falling out of their tie for first place (remember that they own the tiebreaker). Isaac Paredes had put Houston ahead with a solo homer and an RBI knock in the third, but the Astros’ bullpen set that lead on fire. The big blow came off the bat of Ronald Acuña Jr., who belted a grand slam off Bryan Abreu in the seventh after AJ Blubaugh made a right mess of things.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox and Tampa Bay Rays head into Sunday’s series finale at Fenway Park with the three-game set knotted at one win apiece after Saturday’s 2-1 Rays victory.
Left-hander Patrick Sandoval takes the mound for Boston against Tampa Bay right-hander Griffin Jax, a matchup that carries extra weight with the regular season winding down and playoff positioning still in flux.
Interim manager Chad Tracy has kept the bulk of his starting nine intact, but he has made a modest yet noticeable adjustment involving outfielder Jarren Duran, via Underdog MLB.
After sitting out the series opener and batting eighth on Saturday, Duran will slide up one spot into the seventh hole. He will hit in front of Isaiah Kiner-Falefa and Nate Eaton while remaining in center field, the position he has occupied since injuries to Ceddanne Rafaela and Eli White opened the job.
The rest of the order features Roman Anthony in left, Mickey Gasper at designated hitter, Adley Rutschman behind the plate, Trevor Story at shortstop, Nick Sogard at first, and Cooper Durbin at third.
The move comes during a difficult individual season for Duran. Entering Sunday he is hitting .206 in 144 games, with 65 runs, 110 hits, 20 home runs and 69 RBIs. His slugging percentage sits at .364 and his OPS at .626.
Speculation about a possible trade lingered for weeks before the August 4 deadline, yet Duran remained in a Red Sox uniform and has continued to receive regular playing time as the club pushes toward October.
Boston sits at 84-71 with seven games left and occupies what currently looks like the second American League Wild Card spot. Should the standings hold, the Red Sox would open the postseason on the road in a best-of-three Wild Card series against the New York Yankees.
Every remaining game, including Sunday’s finale against a familiar division rival, therefore carries playoff implications.
Tracy’s decision to bump Duran up in the order is a small tactical shift rather than a wholesale overhaul, but it signals a willingness to tinker as the club tries to generate more consistent offense down the stretch.
Whether the extra spot in the lineup produces results remains to be seen.
Duran’s season-long struggles have been well documented, yet he has shown flashes of the power and speed that once made him a fixture in the middle of Boston’s order.
A productive afternoon against Jax and the Rays would give the Red Sox a series victory and a bit of momentum heading into the final week.
With the calendar now late September and the postseason picture still taking shape, even incremental lineup changes can feel significant.

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Richie Palacios dropped a blooper into shallow right in the ninth inning to score Junior Caminero and give the Tampa Bay Rays a 2-1 victory over the Boston Red Sox on Saturday.
Tampa Bay, which has three walk-off wins on its current homestand, lowered its magic number to clinch the AL East to five games. The second-place Yankees are in Arizona on Saturday night.
Prior to Palacios’ single, the Rays were 0 for 17 with runners in scoring position over the first two games of the series. The postseason-bound Rays, who’ve won seven of their last eight, capitalized on two fortuitous bounces in the ninth.
First, Caminero’s foul popup bounced off the Tropicana Field catwalk and out of the reach of third baseman Caleb Durbin. Caminero then lined the next pitch from Garrett Whitlock (7-2) into left. Three batters later, after Chandler Simpson singled, Connor Wong’s passed ball moved Caminero to third.
Bidding to clinch a wild-card berth, the Red Sox squandered a prime opportunity in the top of the ninth.
Facing closer Bryan Baker (4-2) in a tie game, Boston got a double from Caleb Durbin and a triple from Jarren Duran. However, Nick Fortes threw out Durbin stealing third before Duran’s triple, and Caminero made a stellar play at third base to retire Isiah Kiner-Falefa, stranding Duran.
Boston also wasted a phenomenal effort from starter Brayan Bello, who matched a career high with 11 strikeouts. In eight innings, he allowed five hits, one run and no walks. Red Sox closer Aroldis Chapman (lat tightness) was unavailable.
The Red Sox took a 1-0 lead with doubles from Durbin and Roman Anthony in the third inning. Trevor Story extended his hitting streak to 10 games with a sixth-inning single.
Jonathan Aranda tied it with an opposite-field solo homer on the first pitch of the Rays’ fourth.
The Rays are an MLB-best 25-14 in one-run games.
Boston could have clinched a playoff berth with a win combined with a loss by either the Rangers or Astros. Both of those teams were seven games behind the Red Sox with eight games remaining entering Saturday.
UP NEXT
Right-hander Griffin Jax (7-10, 3.80 ERA) gets the nod for the Rays on Sunday in the series finale. Boston had not announced a starter.

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

20 Sep 2026, 04:49 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Kim Klement Neitzel)
Richie Palacios produced a two-out, walk-off single in the ninth inning as the Tampa Bay Rays edged the Boston Red Sox 2-1 on Saturday afternoon in St. Petersburg, Fla., to even their final home series of the regular season.
Against Garrett Whitlock (7-2), Palacios looped a 1-2 sinker into shallow right to score Junior Caminero as the Rays (94-60) hit their third walk-off winner during the nine-game homestand.
Jonathan Aranda homered while Liam Hicks and Chandler Simpson posted two hits apiece as Tampa Bay improved to 7-1 on the homestand.
Bidding for a fifth consecutive win over five starts, Freddy Peralta received no decision after yielding just one run on four hits over 5 2/3 innings that took 97 pitches. He struck out six and walked two.
Caleb Durbin stroked two doubles and scored for the Red Sox (84-71), who lost for the first time in three games.
Starting pitcher Brayan Bello went a season-best eight innings and allowed one run on five hits with a career high-tying 11 strikeouts.
The Rays got an out with the infield drawn in and appeared to escape trouble in the third. Then Roman Anthony, who homered and had three RBIs in Friday's 4-2 win in the opener, remained hot and made it 1-0 with a two-out double that scored Durbin.
Cedric Mullins laid down a bunt single and reached second on Durbin's throwing error to open the third, but he was picked off and caught trying to steal third on Jorge Mateo's failed sacrifice bunt.
In the fourth, Aranda tied it 1-all when he rocked his 22nd homer to left field as he took Bello's 97 m.p.h. four-seam fastball the opposite way.
With Bello still in the game in the seventh, Hicks led off with a single and Simpson dropped one into right with no outs. Following a groundout and a fielder's choice, Bello ended the threat by whiffing Mullins on a foul tip.
Durbin lined his second double with one out in the ninth, but Hicks tossed him out trying to steal third. Jarren Duran followed with his fifth triple, but Isiah Kiner-Falefa grounded out to deep third to end the inning off Bryan Baker (4-2).
--Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
Caleb Durbin managed to do exactly what you do not want to do as the go-ahead run.
The Boston Red Sox played Saturday against the division rival Tampa Bay Rays. In the top of the ninth inning at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Fla. with the score tied 1-1, the Boston infielder Durbin hit a one-out double to represent the winning run.
In the middle of the next at-bat by teammate Jarren Duran however, Durbin committed an inexplicable blunder — he decided to make a break for third base. Durbin was then easily thrown out for the second out of the inning.
Caleb Durbin is caught trying to steal 3rd and Junior Caminero is FIRED UP
We are still tied in the 9th!pic.twitter.com/wrriTXW1yj
Making matters even worse for Durbin was that Duran proceeded to smack a triple in his at-bat (but was stranded at third after Isiah Kiner-Falefa grounded out to end the half-inning). While Duran’s triple would have allowed Durbin to waltz home if he had simply stayed put, the baserunning error left the game tied and opened the door for the Rays to win the game in the bottom of the ninth inning on a walkoff RBI single by Richie Palacios.
It is hard to tell exactly what Durbin was thinking there. He was already in scoring position and also had a left-handed batter up at the plate (meaning that the catcher had an obstructed throw to third base). Though Durbin has stolen 19 bases so far this season, that was simply a risk completely unnecessary for him to take in that situation.
On the bright side, the 84-71 Red Sox do look to be locked into the second AL Wild Card spot at this point, which would have them open up the playoffs against the rival New York Yankees. But these are the types of moments that explain why Boston is a Wild Card team to begin with (similar to the time that they cost themselves four runs by botching a single challenge).

item.content:encoded:
Since he hit Seth Lugo’s fastball, Yordan Alvarez knew that ball was out of the park. The hit came off at 107.2 mph and landed 385 feet into right field, right in the second-level seats at Daikin Park to give Houston a 4-1 lead over the Kansas City Royals earlier this week.
Thus continued Alvarez's pursuit of the Triple Crown—the last one was won by Miguel Cabrera in 2012 with the Detroit Tigers in the American League—, hitting his 40th home run of the season to join a select club in the history of the Astros and players born in Cuba.
He became just the fifth player in Astros history to reach that mark:
• Jeff Bagwell — 47 (2000), 43 (1997), 42 (1999)
• Lance Berkman — 45 (2006), 42 (2002)
• Richard Hidalgo — 44 (2000)
• Alex Bregman — 41 (2019)
• Yordan Alvarez — 40 (2026)
The Hall of Fame member, Jeff Bagwell, was the first Houston hitter to hit 40 or more home runs in a season, when he achieved the feat with 43 home runs in 1997, at 29 years old. In his entire career, he finished recording three similar seasons (1997, 1999 and 2000).
The 47 home runs he hit in the 2000 season remained marked as the most in club history. Richard Hidalgo (44 HR in 2000) and Alex Bregman (41 in 2019) have been the youngest hitters to enter the club, both at 25 years old. But this season, he has made the difference in an unprecedented season for a 40-home-run hitter who has worn the Astros uniform, as he leads the league with an offensive line of .311/.429/.598, 1.027 OPS, 189 OPS+, 319 total bases, 103 walks and 32 intentional walks.
After going through a slump in his home run production, with only five in the last 40 games, Alvarez has heated up again with a pair of home runs in his last 10 at-bats, both in the series that Houston won 2-1 against the Royals. Now he is one home run away from tying Tampa Bay Rays third baseman Junior Caminero, who leads the American League with 41, and three RBIs away from reaching Pete Alonso (102).
Houston has eight games remaining to finish the regular season, two more against the Atlanta Braves at home, a two-game road trip against the Seattle Mariners and four against the Athletics.
Another Chapter of Glory Among Cuban Hitters
Alvarez also joined the list of only four Cuban-born hitters who have hit at least 40 home runs in the Majors. The legendary Cooperstown Hall of Fame member, Tony Pérez, was the first Cuban-born hitter to hit at least 40 home runs in a season, when he reached the milestone in the 1970 season with the Cincinnati Reds’ “Big Red Machine.”
Eighteen years later, José Canseco appears on the historical list, at just 23 years old, in his historic 40-40 season (42 home runs and 40 stolen bases), wearing the Oakland Athletics uniform in 1988.
Canseco entered the club four times, repeating the feat with 41 home runs in 1991 and 46 in 1998. Another who reached the milestone was Rafael Palmeiro, who leads the group of Cuban hitters with four 40-home-run seasons (1998-1999 and 2000 and 2002). Seventeen years later, Jorge Soler hit 48 home runs with the Royals and took ownership of the record for Cubans in a single season, leaving behind Palmeiro’s 47-home-run seasons in 1999 and 2001.
For the first time in the club, Alvarez can go much farther if he manages to regain his home run pace in these last nine games. Before reaching the August and September stretch, his worst month in production had been June when he hit six home runs in 26 games. However, as we saw before, he has been able to take only five balls out of the park since August 1 until now, and that has made the race against Caminero become much more attractive.
Alvarez still has the possibility of reaching a Triple Crown by leading all three offensive categories in all of MLB, a feat that no hitter has accomplished since Mickey Mantle with the New York Yankees in 1956 (.353 BA, 52 HR, 130 RBI).

He currently writes for Diamond Centric, where he covers the New York Mets, San Diego Padres, Chicago Cubs, Milwaukee Brewers, and Kansas City Royals. My work focuses on game coverage, player analysis, and storytelling that connects performance with context. My Substack has also been an important part of my writing development, where I’ve built much of my baseball coverage and storytelling voice over time. I’m passionate about combining reporting, research, and thoughtful analysis to produce engaging baseball content for readers.

item.content:encoded:
For the second straight year, Tampa Bay Rays’ Junior Caminero has proven that he’s one of the game’s most talented hitters. He’s played two full seasons in the Big Leagues and has hit 40+ home runs in each of those seasons.
At just 23 years old, Caminero continues to show the league day in and day out that he’s one of the most exciting young phenoms in the league. Not only is he making a case for himself as an American League MVP candidate, but he’s having all this success on one of the best teams in the league. The Rays have the best record in the AL and have 93 wins.
A key reason for the immense success he’s had, particularly this past season, is his elite bat speed. Pair that with all of the other attributes he brings to the table, including his plate discipline, strength, quick hands, natural ability and his ability to adjust quickly, and Caminero’s future is as bright as anyone’s in the league.
Caminero’s average bat speed this season is 79.6 mph, the top mark among all 202 qualified hitters in the entire league, according to Statcast. For context as to how good this really is, the average bat speed for players in the league is about 72 mph.
Swing speed is key to Junior Caminero's success
“It’s his bat speed,” Tampa Bay’s manager Kevin Cash said. “I don’t know if anybody swings harder, quicker, whatever you want to do, in baseball.”
Cash added: “So it allows him to muscle through pitches. … He’s not squaring every single ball up. It’s just that he’s so quick getting the barrel through the zone. And it’s level enough to where he can cover a lot of different pitches at different angles. It’s not in and out of the zone."
When it comes to specific studies of his swing, Caminero’s flat, level swing is also a primary factor in his success. His swing has a vertical tilt of 25 degrees, according to Statcast. There are only four players in the league who have flatter swings than Caminero, as his swing ranks fifth in all of baseball in terms of angle and levelness.
Caminero spoke about how elite his numbers are and how he’s been able to achieve such incredible marks with stats including bat speed, bat angle and swing length, which is the longest in the league at 8.7 feet.
“God-given ability,” Caminero said. “God blessed me. I mean, thank God for this. We used to pray for this.”
He added: “It’s cool, because when somebody tells you that you have the fastest swing in the league, I say, ‘Wow!’ “When you see Aaron Judge, when you see Giancarlo Stanton, when you see Vladimir Guerrero (Jr.), you see Oneil Cruz, it’s the best, to be honest, to be within this group.”
Caminero’s teammate Drew Rasmussen spoke about the rare ability and talent that Caminero possesses.
“It’s unbelievable what he can do,” Rasmussen said. “It’s unbelievable how young he is, the maturity level that he possesses and his understanding and just how he’s grown into being a really, really good Major League Baseball player at the age of 23.”
Rasmussen revealed how he’d plan to pitch to Caminero if he were to face him.
“If we had to face him, I think I’d throw him four sliders in the left-handed batter’s box and hope he swings,” Rasmussen said. “And if he takes, he gets to go to first base. I mean, it’s better than giving up a homer.”
“It’s incredible,” Rasmussen added. “It’s just one of those things that every swing, regardless of pitch location, has the opportunity to (do) damage.”
Caminero’s stellar bat speed, as well as his swing level, are the core reasons for his abundance of success over the past two years for the Rays. He will look to continue that success in the regular season’s final weeks and into the postseason, as Tampa Bay makes its first postseason appearance since 2023.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yordan Alvarez vs. Junior Caminero for AL MVP: Can a designated hitter win the award?

item.content:encoded:
Yordan Alvarez has been the American League's best hitter in 2026. But is that enough for him to be crowned AL MVP? The Astros' designated hitter has one week left to hold off young Rays superstar Junior Caminero, who has made a surge for the award in recent weeks.
There's no denying that the Astros' slugger has had a monster season, hitting .311 with 40 homers and 99 RBI in 149 games entering Friday. He currently leads the AL in on-base percentage (.429), slugging (.598) and OPS (1.027). And he has stayed healthy and played in all but four of Houston's games, allowing him to put together a remarkable season.
When it comes to winning MVP, the numbers are critically important, and the narrative of the season plays a part as well. But an often overlooked aspect of award voting, particularly for MVP, is historical precedent.
Alvarez is a primary designated hitter, and prior to Shohei Ohtani's historic 50/50 season in 2024, in which he did not pitch but won NL MVP, no primary DH had ever won the MVP Award. Ohtani in 2024 is still the only DH to do it, given that in his other MVP seasons, he also pitched.
Considering his singular status as a two-way player, Ohtani is the exception to this rule. Besides him, no full-time designated hitter has ever won MVP. In fact, since 2000, only six designated hitters have finished in the top five of MVP voting. That list includes Frank Thomas (second in 2000, fourth in 2006), David Ortiz (fifth in 2003, fourth in 2004, second in 2005, third in 2006, fourth in 2007), Travis Hafner (fifth in 2005), J.D. Martinez (fourth in 2018), Marcell Ozuna (fourth in 2024) and Kyle Schwarber (second in 2025). Alvarez finished third in 2022 while splitting time between DH and outfield.
Among designated hitters since 1995, here are five of the top seasons comparable to Alvarez's 2026 and where they finished in MVP balloting:
- Edgar Martinez, 1995: .356/.479/.628, 182 H, 29 HR, 113 RBI, 182 wRC+, 7.0 fWAR — third
- Frank Thomas, 2000: .328/.436/.625, 191 H, 43 HR, 143 RBI, 160 wRC+, 5.9 fWAR — second
- David Ortiz, 2005: .300/.397/.604, 180 H, 47 HR, 148 RBI, 157 wRC+, 5.3 fWAR — second
- David Ortiz, 2007: .332/.445/.621, 182 H, 35 HR, 117 RBI, 175 wRC+, 6.3 fWAR — fourth
- J.D. Martinez, 2018: .330/.402/.629, 188 H, 43 HR, 130 RBI, 170 wRC+, 5.8 fWAR — fourth
- Yordan Alvarez, 2026: 311/.429/.598, 166 H, 40 HR, 99 RBI, 177 wRC+, 6.2 fWAR — ?
When you look at what Alvarez has accomplished this season, his numbers with eight games to play are right in line with those of his elite DH contemporaries. But if designated hitters who put up similar seasons weren't able to win MVP, will the Astros' slugger be able to reverse that trend?
Short of playing a defensive position, Alvarez has done everything he can to hold off Caminero, but the Rays' third baseman has made a push over the past month. The 23-year-old, who has earned the title of best player on the AL's best team, is slashing .277/.363/.532 with 41 home runs and 96 RBI this season. Although he rates out poorly defensively, Caminero has appeared in 151 games and counting at the hot corner. Plus, he delivered his potential MVP moment with a walk-off homer to clinch a playoff berth for the Rays.
One of the things working against Alvarez is the fact that, after being on pace to do so for most of the season, he is now unlikely to win the AL Triple Crown. Entering Friday, he's tied with Tampa Bay's Chandler Simpson for the league lead in batting average, he's second to Caminero in home runs, and he's second in RBI behind Baltimore's Pete Alonso.
Recent history tells us that a historic season, like Ohtani's 50/50 season in 2024 or Aaron Judge's AL-record 61 home runs in 2022, can provide the narrative juice to pave the way to MVP, making the Triple Crown Alvarez's best path to the award this year. Only Miguel Cabrera in 2012 has accomplished that feat in the past 60 years. Without the Triple Crown, it'll likely be tougher for Alvarez to sway voters.
Another thing that's likely hurting Alvarez's case is how poorly the Astros have played in 2026. They might be one of the worst division winners in MLB history, or they could still miss the postseason completely. That said, there's precedent for this in recent MVP voting, as Bryce Harper won the 2021 NL MVP Award on an 82-80 Phillies team that missed the postseason.
Over the past six seasons, the AL MVP Award has been dominated by Ohtani and Judge, with very little argument in the years they've won. But this season, with Alvarez and Caminero, voters will be selecting a new winner, and they'll have to decide what's most important in determining most valuable.
For the Astros' slugger, we'll wait to see if a nearly historic season by a designated hitter can be enough.

item.content:encoded:
The Triple Crown in the baseball world is a bit of an old-school feat, but it is a feat that very rarely happens these days, nonetheless. No hitter has won a Triple Crown since Miguel Cabrera pulled it off in 2012. Cabrera's feat was the first since 1967. A Triple Crown is leading your respective league in batting average, home runs and RBI. As noted, it's a bit old school because batting average isn't the most preferred rate stat and people have also shifted attention away from RBI.
Still, it's really cool to track when someone is close, and Astros outfielder and AL MVP frontrunner Yordan Alvarez has a real shot as the 2026 season winds down.
Heading into the penultimate weekend of the 2026 MLB season, here are the leaderboards, with Alvarez sitting in the top two of each category.
AL batting average leaders
1. Yordan Alvarez, Astros: .311 (.311444)
2. Chandler Simpson, Rays: .311 (.310661)
3. Yandy Díaz, Rays: .295
AL home run runs
1. Junior Caminero, Rays, 41
2. Yordan Alvarez, Astros, 40
3. Ben Rice, Yankees, 38
4. Pete Alonso, Orioles, 37
AL RBI leaders
1. Pete Alonso, Orioles, 102
2. Yordan Alvarez, Astros, 99
3. Junior Caminero, Rays, 96
4. Jo Adell, Guardians, 92
5. Ben Rice, Yankees, 92
As illustrated, all are tight races. It's possible Alvarez ends up leading the AL in none of the three categories, but he's right on the precipice of having a lead in all three.
Coincidentally, the last six Triple Crown winners in MLB have all been on the AL side. No National League player has won the Triple Crown since Hall of Famer Joe "Ducky" Medwick in 1937. Since then, the AL has seen Ted Williams (1942 and 1947), Mickey Mantle (1956), Frank Robinson (1966), Carl Yastrzemski (1967) and Miguel Cabrera (2012) pull it off.
No Astros player has ever won the Triple Crown.
Yordan Alvarez Triple Crown prediction
Could Alvarez become the first? The Astros -- who are clinging to the lead in the AL West -- and Alvarez have nine games remaining: they host the Braves for a three-game set this weekend before closing the regular season with a six-game road trip in Seattle (two games) and Sacramento (four games)
The two games in Seattle bring a difficult ballpark, but with three home games and finishing with four in Sacramento's Sutter Health Park, the conditions seem ripe for a strong finish. I'll predict that he gets the job done and wins the Triple Crown.

item.title: [NBC Sports] The 2026 MLB Season from A to Z: Yordan Alvarez, PCA, Jacob Misiorowski and more

item.description:
Many fans rely on numbers to tell the story of a baseball season. For 2026, I’m going with letters. Here’s the story of the regular season from A to Z.
A: Yordan Alvarez: He’s the only qualifier in baseball with an OBP of over .400. He’s leading the American League in batting, on-base, slugging, OPS, and walks. item.content:encoded:
Many fans rely on numbers to tell the story of a baseball season. For 2026, I’m going with letters. Here’s the story of the regular season from A to Z.

A: Yordan Alvarez: He’s the only qualifier in baseball with an OBP of over .400. He’s leading the American League in batting, on-base, slugging, OPS, and walks. Where would Joe Espada’s Astros be without him? Yordan is still the favorite to win the American League MVP, despite his numbers falling off a bit down the stretch.
B: Bryan Baker: Tampa Bay scored 698 runs and allowed 618 in games through September 17. That would give them a record of 84-68 according to the Pythagorean Theorem. But they were 93-59, nine games better. Credit in part goes to their closer Baker, leading the league with 40 saves this season..
C: Pete Crow-Armstrong: When the Cubs suffered through a 10-game losing streak in May, Pete batted just .161 (5-36 AB) in those 10 games. In games through September 17, PCA in 85 Cubs victories: .357/.442/.740. He scored 89 runs in 85 Cubs wins. The NL MVP by a mile. You cannot tell the story of the 2026 season without talking about Pete Crow-Armstrong.
D: Jacob deGrom: On September 10, deGrom started against the Mariners in Seattle. In six innings, he faced just 19 batters, one over the minimum. He struck out 12, gave up one hit, walked none, and didn’t allow a run. He left the game with Texas leading by three runs. The bullpen flushed away the lead and Texas wound up losing the game. The story of deGrom’s career. Jacob is historically significant. He has started 277 games in his career, and three of his top 10 (ranked by Pitchers’ Game Score) have come in 2026.
E: Errors: There’s only been one season EVER with fewer errors per game than 2026. Of course, that would be 2025. No pitcher has made more than four errors this season. In 1969, Jim Kaat won a Gold Glove, despite making eight errors (tied for the MLB lead with Boston’s Ray Culp among pitchers). Gold Gloves were all reputation in those days. In fact, Kaat’s longtime Minnesota teammate, Zoilo Versalles, won a Gold Glove in 1965 despite making 39 errors!
F: Freddie Freeman: Freeman has hit 32 doubles this year and 579 in his career. Is 579 doubles a lot? Well, that’s 90 more than the next-closest active player, Paul Goldschmidt. And when Freddie legs out his 600th, he’ll become only the 19th player with at least 600 doubles. He’s a little more than a season away from passing both Hank Aaron (624) and Barry Bonds (601).
G: Vladimir Guerrero Jr.: Vlad Jr. hit a home run every 25 at-bats in 2025. He’s hit a home run every 58 at-bats in 2026. He didn’t hit his first home run at home this year until Toronto’s 75th home game. He had gone 84 straight home games without a homer.
H: Bryce Harper: In March, Harper hit a two-run game-tying homer in the 8th inning of the WBC Finals. This season, his wRC+ (139) has been one of the top dozen in the majors. In October, can he lead the Phillies to his first World Series championship?
I: Raisel Iglesias: The Braves have spent all season in first place, and Iglesias is a big part of that. In the last 10 years (2017-2026) only one player (Kenley Jansen) has more saves than Iglesias. He’s 33-for-36 in save chances this year for the Braves. But here’s the thing: over the last five years, he’s saved 130 games for the Braves, but only one in the postseason. That has to change.
J: Aaron Judge: #99 missed 99 days (84 games) this season with a rib injury, but the three-time MVP came back in mid-September with enough time to get his timing back at the plate. Yankees fans will have to hope that the leg tightness isn’t a big deal.
K: Steven Kwan: There hasn’t been a hotter hitter in the American League since the start of July. Kwan is batting .350 since July 1, and .351 since the All-Star break. The Guardians have needed every bit of his offense, as José Ramírez has not been the same since returning from his broken left hamate bone.
L: Brandon Lowe: In his first season with Pittsburgh, Lowe has hit a career best 30 homers and has an OPS over .800. The Pirates offense was one of the big stories of the first half of the 2026 season, and Lowe was a big reason why. In the second half, injuries to Oneil Cruz and Ryan O’Hearn have sunk the Bucs but the offense was fun while it lasted.
M: Jacob Misiorowski: Milwaukee has the best record in baseball, and he’s a big reason why. Has any Brewers pitcher ever had a better season than the 24-year-old ace? Sorry, fans of Teddy Higuera. The answer is no. “The Miz” leads the majors in strikeouts (243). He leads the majors in ERA (1.89). He’s striking out more than 13 batters per nine innings! Misiorowski has had 1,053 pitches this season over 100.0 mph. No one else in pitch tracking era (2008-present) has had a season of 1,000 or more.
N: No-Hitters: On May 25, three Astros pitchers Tatsuya Imai (6 IP), Steven Okert (1 IP), and Alimber Santa (2 IP) combined to complete the Astros’ fifth combined no-hitter in franchise history. No one pitcher has completed a no-hitter since Blake Snell did it in August of 2024 for the Giants.
O: Shohei Ohtani: There are two players whose last name starts with “O” with more homers than Ohtani this season: Matt Olson and Kazuma Okamoto. But Ohtani made 14 brilliant starts (1.79 ERA) and his wRC+ of 142 is in the top 10 in the game.
P: Salvador Perez: The 36-year-old put up nearly 600 at-bats this season. And while most of them came as a DH or 1B, he did start 44 games behind the plate. In his 15-year career, he’s caught 1,427 games (1,396 starts) and nearly 12,000 innings.
Q: Quick games: On September 7, in an afternoon game at Citizens Bank Park, the Phillies beat the Braves 1-0 in a game that took 1:51 to play. On June 16 at Dodger Stadium, the Dodgers defeated the Rays 1-0 in a game that took 1:52 to complete. And in early April, the Royals defeated the White Sox in games on April 10 and 11 that lasted in 1:54 and 1:55, respectively. Thank you, pitch clock.
R: Eduardo Rodriguez: The Diamondbacks have won 22 of E-Rod’s first 30 starts. Talk about valuable! He has a 2.62 ERA this season (it was 5.04 and 5.02 in the two previous seasons). This is his best year since 2019.
S: Cam Schlittler: Is he the AL MVP, or just the AL Cy Young? The Yankees won 20 of his 31 starts. The Yankees don’t need a lot of offense when he takes the mound. He has a 1.14 ERA in 16 road starts this season! Since earned runs became official in both leagues in 1913, Schlittler’s 1.14 road ERA is the fourth best (minimum 15 road starts). The top three: Bob Gibson in 1968 (0.81 ERA); Walter Johnson in 1913 (1.06 ERA); and Greg Maddux in 1995 (1.12 ERA).
T: Bruce Turang: What a player! His OPS has gone up in each of his first four seasons. He’s now a 20 HR/20 SB/100 runs/100 RBI player. The Brewers need him to improve his performance in last year’s NLCS vs. the Dodgers, when he went 1-for-15 (.067).
U: Uncle Charlie (curveball): The curveball is heading toward extinction, much like individual no-hitters. Curveballs have only accounted for 6.4% of pitches this season, the second lowest rate since first tracked in 2008 (2024: 6.1%). That’s pure curves, not including slow curves or knuckle-curves. Want to know which pitcher has thrown the most curveballs (including knuckle and slow curves) this year? Philadelphia’s Aaron Nola, at 942.
V: Miguel Vargas: The White Sox have been one of the best stories this year, and we could have given the “V” to manager Max Venable. But Vargas’ 31 home runs and stealing 19 bases in 21 attempts makes him the choice. Vargas has a 4.7 WAR this season, up from 1.9 last year.
W: Willson and Wilyer, the heart of the Boston lineup. Right fielder Wilyer Abreu leads the American League with 36 doubles. He also leads the AL in outfield assists with 12. Willson Contreras has an OPS of .905, second in AL to Alvarez, even ahead of Rays slugger Junior Caminero. Remember, Boston was 14 games under .500 as late as June 24. And then the season turned around.
X: Xander Bogaerts: The Padres have played well down the stretch and now appear likely to reach the postseason. And X-Man has contributed, stealing 21 bases in 22 attempts this year. It’s no fluke, either. He stole 20 of 22 last season. In his four seasons with the Padres, he has stolen 73 bases in 81 attempts. That’s efficiency.
Y: Yoshinobu Yamamoto: The Dodgers’ Yoshinobu Yamamoto has a 1.98 ERA in 10 starts after the All-Star break. He’s probably the key to the Dodgers’ chances of completing a three-peat. Who can forget what he did last October, when he went 5-1, with a 1.45 ERA in 37.1 postseason innings.
Z: Zack Wheeler: From July 21 through August 24, Wheeler had a stretch of seven starts that saw him give up 26 runs (25 earned) in 31.1 innings (7.18 ERA). He was terrific in the first half and recaptured his form down the stretch. If the Phillies are going to go deep into October, they’ll need Wheeler (and their other two aces) to be at the top of their game.
Editors’ Note: Elliott Kalb - dubbed “Mr. Stats” decades ago by Marv Albert and Bob Costas - is the former Senior Editorial Director at MLB Network and a longtime contributor of research and information to NBC Sports’ telecasts.
